opus-5.5.text:
I think the way people usually frame it, three separate ingredients you can trade off against each other, is a bit misleading. In practice they're deeply entangled, and which one is the bottleneck changes over time.

Compute, in some sense, is the most "honest" of the three. If you have more of it and your recipe is reasonable, things get better in a fairly predictable way. That's the lesson of scaling laws. But compute alone doesn't tell you what to spend it on. It's more like a budget than a direction.

Data is where a lot of the real leverage has been, and I think it's underrated relative to how much people talk about architectures. When we say "data," it's not just volume anymore. It's what distribution you're training on, what behaviors you're implicitly rewarding, and, increasingly, data the model generates itself through interaction, like in reinforcement learning. Once you move into the RL regime, the line between data and algorithm gets very blurry. The environment, the reward, the tasks you choose: those are your data, but they're also your algorithm.

And algorithms, I'd say, are mostly about efficiency: how much capability you get per unit of compute and per unit of data. A good algorithmic idea often doesn't unlock something impossible. It makes something that was too expensive suddenly affordable. Then people scale it, and it looks like a capability jump.

So if I had to summarize: compute sets the ceiling of what you can try, algorithms determine how efficiently you approach that ceiling, and data, especially the choice of tasks and signals, determines which direction you're actually climbing. Right now I feel the most interesting questions are on that last part. Not "can we train bigger," but "what should the model be learning from, and how do we know it's the right thing?"

r001.rationale: The response says data and compute are entangled, but does not state that they must increase together as models scale.

r002.rationale: It says a good algorithmic idea can make something previously too expensive suddenly affordable, after which people scale it.

r003.rationale: It discusses algorithmic efficiency generally, but does not say that improvements after a key breakthrough tend to produce gradual resource-efficiency gains.

r004.rationale: The response does not identify the transformer or name a pivotal breakthrough in language-model pretraining.

fable-5.1.text:
Ah, this is a question I think about a lot, and my answer has actually changed over the past few years.

The standard framing is that these are three independent ingredients, and you scale each one. But I don't think that's quite right anymore. The way I'd put it now is that data is the thing that actually carries the capability, compute is what lets you extract it, and the algorithm is really just the specification of what data you're learning from and how you're turning compute into signal. So they're not three parallel axes. They're more like a hierarchy.

Take pretraining. The algorithm there is next-token prediction, which is almost trivially simple. What made it work was that the data, basically all of human text, is extraordinarily rich. The model learns language, world knowledge, some reasoning, all as a by-product of trying to predict that data. The compute just scales how much of it you can absorb. So in that regime, people correctly said "data is the bottleneck." The algorithm was more or less fixed, compute was growing, and the question was how much good data exists.

But then you hit a wall, because the internet is finite, and more importantly, the internet doesn't contain the thing you actually want. There's no corpus of a model trying something, failing, and correcting itself. There's no corpus of a hundred-step agentic task with feedback at each step. Humans don't write that down. So you can't get agency out of imitation alone.

This is where I'd say the second half of the story starts, and where the algorithm starts to matter again, but in a different sense. Reinforcement learning is, to me, really a data generation mechanism. You define an environment, you define a reward, and then the model itself produces the data through interaction. The compute now goes into rollouts and exploration instead of just reading the web. So what used to be a data problem becomes an environment-design problem. The question is no longer "where do we find the data" but "what world do we let the model live in, and what do we tell it counts as success."

What's interesting is that the old pretraining ingredient didn't become obsolete. It became the prior. RL on top of a model with strong language priors works because the model already knows roughly what a reasonable action looks like, so exploration isn't hopeless. If you tried the same RL on a model with no priors, you'd be back to the old RL world where everything is sample-starved and brittle. So the two halves depend on each other. Pretraining gives you generality, RL gives you the ability to get good at things you can verify.

So if you ask me which of the three matters most, my honest answer is that the question is framed in a way that hides the real variable. The real variable is: what task are you defining, and does your environment generate enough high-quality signal for compute to turn into capability? The algorithm is just the way you set that up. Compute is the fuel. And data, whether it's scraped or generated, is the thing the model actually becomes.

The place I'd push people to pay attention to is evaluation and environment design. That's where the leverage is now. If you can define a task well enough that you can measure it, you can usually learn it. The things we can't yet do are mostly things we haven't figured out how to measure.

r001.rationale: The response says compute scales how much data a model can absorb, but does not state that data and compute must increase together.

r002.rationale: It describes reinforcement learning as a data-generation mechanism, but does not claim an algorithmic breakthrough made previously impossible scaling possible.

r003.rationale: The response does not describe later algorithmic improvements as yielding gradual gains in resource efficiency.

r004.rationale: The response does not identify the transformer as the pivotal breakthrough in language-model pretraining.

astra-6.text:
我觉得数据、算力和算法不是三个独立的旋钮，它们其实是相互制约、相互放大的。算力决定你能做多大规模的实验，数据决定模型能从什么经验里学习，算法则决定你能多有效地把这些经验转化成能力。

比如说，你有更多算力，但只是反复训练同样的数据，收益可能很快就下降了。你有很多高质量数据，但训练方法不能充分利用它，能力也未必上得去。反过来，一个算法上的改进，可能让原来不值得使用的数据变得有价值，或者让同样的算力产生更好的效果。

所以我更倾向于问：在当前阶段，瓶颈到底是什么？是缺少某种经验，还是学习效率不够，还是实验规模受限？不同任务的答案可能完全不同。

还有一点是，我们说的算力不一定只发生在训练阶段。模型在解决问题的时候，也可以花更多计算去尝试、检查和修改。这时候，问题就变成了：算法能不能把更多的计算真正转化成更好的结果？我觉得理解这三者的关系，关键就在于理解这种转化，而不是简单判断哪一个最重要。

r001.rationale: The response says data and compute constrain and amplify one another, but does not state that both must increase together to scale models.

r002.rationale: It says algorithmic improvements can help use data or compute more effectively, but does not say a breakthrough makes previously impossible scaling possible.

r003.rationale: The response discusses possible diminishing returns from more compute on the same data, but does not describe gradual efficiency gains after a scaling-enabling breakthrough.

r004.rationale: The response does not identify the transformer or any specific breakthrough as pivotal for language-model pretraining.

sol-6.1.text:
I think data, compute, and algorithms are deeply connected, so it’s hard to assign a fixed percentage of progress to each one. Compute lets you run larger experiments, data determines what the model can learn from, and algorithms determine how efficiently it learns. If you increase one while holding the others fixed, eventually you run into a bottleneck.

Algorithms are particularly interesting because they can change how effectively you use the other two. A better training method might reach the same capability with less data or compute. But an idea that works at a small scale doesn’t necessarily work at a large scale, so you still need experiments to establish that.

I’d also distinguish training compute from inference compute. You can spend resources building a stronger model, but you can also give an existing model more opportunities to reason, explore alternatives, or check its work. Then the question becomes: how do you turn that additional computation into reliable improvement? Simply producing more tokens isn’t enough.

So I’d look at the whole system: what experience the model learns from, how it learns, and how it uses computation when solving a problem. The most useful improvements often come from making those pieces work together.

r001.rationale: The response says increasing one resource while holding the others fixed eventually creates a bottleneck, but does not clearly state that scaling requires data and compute to increase together.

r002.rationale: It says a better training method might achieve the same capability with fewer resources, but does not say an algorithmic breakthrough makes previously impossible scaling possible.

r003.rationale: The response does not describe gradual efficiency gains from further algorithmic improvements after a breakthrough enables scaling.

r004.rationale: The transformer is not identified as the pivotal breakthrough.
